faqs.q: Groundhogs are undermining my Prince Frederick shed — what is involved?
faqs.a: Around Prince Frederick, groundhogs dig where fields meet yards, and a burrow system under a shed or barn slab can have three or four entrances spread across a fence line. We trap at the active entrances through the spring-to-fall season, then backfill the tunnels and screen the slab edge so the next groundhog cannot reopen the system. Groundhogs are among the species the Maryland Department of Health lists as commonly testing positive for rabies in the state, so animals are handled with appropriate caution and never cornered by hand. Landowners may legally address damage-causing groundhogs on their own property, but mapping a multi-entrance system is where most DIY efforts stall.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Prince Frederick?
faqs.a: Prince Frederick work ranges wider than in the suburbs to the north because the properties do. A squirrel in a subdivision attic off Route 4 is a contained job; a farmhouse with bats in the peak, raccoons in the chimney, and groundhog burrows under two outbuildings is a half-day of inspection before the scope is even clear. Travel between spread-out lots and the number of structures on the property both factor in. We inspect every structure you are concerned about, explain the findings building by building, and give you one complete figure before removal or sealing begins.

Prince Frederick.wildlife_intro:
Prince Frederick is Calvert County's seat and its commercial center, but step off Route 4 and the town is still tobacco-country Maryland: farmhouses and newer subdivisions share roads with working fields, and Battle Creek and the county's deep ravines cut wooded corridors between them. That farm-suburb seam is groundhog country first — burrows under the barns, sheds, and deck edges of the larger lots are the most common warm-season call.

Raccoons den in the chimneys of the older homes in town and in the hollow trees of the ravine woods, entering attics where subdivisions back onto those corridors near the high school and the fairgrounds side of town. Bats roost in the big attics of the farmhouses and in the older commercial buildings along Main Street, and skunks work the lawns of the in-town streets each summer. The county's rapid growth along the Route 2/4 corridor keeps pushing new construction into old habitat, so even five-year-old subdivisions here get raccoon and squirrel calls that feel like they belong to farm country. Prince Frederick inspections start outside: outbuildings, burrow systems, and the treeline usually explain the attic animal before we ever climb a ladder.

faqs.q: We only use our Solomons home seasonally — how do we keep animals out over winter?
faqs.a: Seasonal homes on Solomons Island and the Dowell side are the highest-risk properties we see in Calvert County, because an entry chewed in November goes unnoticed until April. The winter pattern is a full exclusion before you close up: chimney capped, vents screened with anchored mesh, soffit and roof-junction gaps sealed, and crawlspace doors latched and framed. Squirrels and raccoons do the most damage, and a raccoon that winters in an attic leaves contamination that needs cleanup, not just removal. A late-winter check, before spring denning starts, catches any new chewing while the fix is still small.

faqs.q: Raccoons are raiding the marina area near my Solomons home — can they be removed?
faqs.a: The raccoons working Solomons' marinas and restaurant blocks are fed by fish scraps, crab waste, and open dumpsters, and they den in the nearest quiet structure — often a cottage attic, boathouse, or crawlspace. We remove animals that have taken up residence in a building and seal that building against re-entry, and we will tell you honestly that shoreline trapping alone does not hold while the food remains. Maryland law prohibits relocating raccoons, so the lasting answer pairs removal from structures with securing the waste that draws them: lidded dumpsters, no fish scraps left out, and pet food brought in at night.

Solomons.wildlife_intro:
Solomons is a narrow island-and-peninsula village where the Patuxent River meets the Chesapeake Bay, and nearly every home is within a few hundred feet of a shoreline, a marina, or a marsh. Raccoons here are practically a waterfront utility: they live in the marsh edges and hollow trees, work the crab pots, fish scraps, and trash around the marinas and restaurants, and den in the attics and crawlspaces of the cottages along the island streets.

The housing layers a working-waterfront village — older frame cottages, watermen's homes, and boathouses — against newer waterfront construction on the mainland side around Dowell and the river shore. Skunks and opossums den under the raised cottages and porch decks, bats summer in the older rooflines and in the quiet attics of seasonal homes, and rats hold on around the marina and restaurant blocks where food waste is constant. Seasonal occupancy is the Solomons multiplier: a home empty from October to April can host a whole winter of squirrel or raccoon activity that the owners discover in a single disastrous spring weekend. Pre-season inspections in late winter are the pattern that works here, sealing the house before the denning season rather than cleaning up after it.
